target.title: fix(anthropic): reject invalid Claude session cursors
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes Claude session pagination accepting malformed opaque cursors as though the cursor were omitted, which could silently restart a catalog at the first page or a transcript at the latest page.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Anthropic plugin now has one exact cursor validator shared by local catalog and transcript requests, gateway host cursor maps, public provider reads, node-host commands, and paired-node responses. A cursor is optional only when absent; present tokens must be non-empty, bounded to 256 UTF-16 code units, and free of surrounding whitespace. Valid opaque tokens remain byte-for-byte unchanged.

The maintainer rewrite also rejects malformed paired-node response cursors instead of trimming or silently dropping them. Catalog failures stay isolated to the affected node host, while transcript failures keep the existing invalid-page error boundary.

## User Impact

Operators browsing Claude session history now receive a clear invalid-cursor failure for malformed pagination state instead of misleading reset or prematurely exhausted results. Valid generated cursors and first-page requests are unchanged.

## Evidence

- Exact head: `9971806660ff4847e5c011a9d2d3623a8b50af16`.

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where five Slack reaction assertions in the tool-result suite intermittently observed zero reaction calls during the full Slack test lane, despite the underlying turn reaching the reply resolver. The failures reproduced on clean `main` in 2 of 3 full-suite runs.

target.title: fix(context-engine): bound deferred turn maintenance with a per-task timeout (AI-assisted)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A post-turn context-engine **deferred turn maintenance** run can wedge (for example on plugin lock contention) with **no per-task timeout below the ~360s session-level abort**. While it is wedged it holds its maintenance lane, so a user message queued behind it on the same session can wait minutes before being processed, even though the model is healthy. `session.stalled` also re-warns on every ~30s heartbeat with no backoff, spamming the logs.

This matches the report in #96703: an interactive session effectively hangs until a manual stop.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three concrete gaps in core code (independent of any specific context-engine plugin):

1. **No per-task timeout was available on the maintenance enqueue.** `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance` enqueued the maintenance worker via `enqueueCommandInLane(...)` with no options. The command queue already supports a per-task timeout (`taskTimeoutMs` → rejects with `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` and releases the lane), but the maintenance lane never wired it up, so an operator hitting the wedge had no knob below the session-level abort.
2. **A timed-out maintenance worker was not fenced.** Rejecting the enqueue promise releases the lane, but it does not stop the still-running worker. A wedged worker could later call `runtimeContext.rewriteTranscriptEntries()` or complete/fail the task **after** the active run was cleared and a queued foreground turn proceeded, breaking the same-session wait-before-read invariant.
3. **`session.stalled` had no log backoff.** `session.stuck` and `session.long_running` already throttle repeats; `session.stalled` did not.

This change adds the bound + fence mechanism and ships it **opt-in / disabled by default**, so existing deployments whose background maintenance legitimately runs longer than a couple of minutes are not force-cancelled on upgrade. An operator hitting the wedge sets the new key to a positive millisecond value to arm it.

## User Impact

- **No behavior change on upgrade unless configured.** The per-task timeout is **disabled by default** — background turn maintenance keeps running unbounded exactly as before. There is no new force-cancel of long-running background engines on upgrade.
- Operators experiencing the wedge **opt in** by setting `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` to a positive millisecond value (absent or `0` keeps it disabled). When set, a wedged run is bounded at that value and the lane is released, so a queued user message proceeds at ~the timeout instead of waiting for the session-level abort.
- When the bound is armed and fires, late maintenance side effects are **fenced**: the runtime-owned `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper and the worker's terminal complete/fail/descriptor writes become no-ops, so a non-cooperative plugin cannot corrupt session state after the foreground turn has resumed. When the bound is disabled, the fence is never armed.
- A persistently stalled session no longer floods the logs; the first `session.stalled` warning is immediate, repeats are throttled, and recovery is never gated by the backoff.

### Changes

- `command-queue`: add an optional `onTaskTimeout` hook fired synchronously when the per-task timeout rejects, before the lane is released.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: resolve an **opt-in** per-task timeout from `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` (absent / `0` / non-positive ⇒ no bound, no fence); when a positive value is set, pass `taskTimeoutMs` + `onTaskTimeout` to the deferred maintenance enqueue and trip a per-run fence on timeout (hook + defensive trip in the timeout catch); thread the fence into the worker and the runtime-context `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper (checked at entry, inside the session-manager rewrite lock, and before the runtime-transcript write) and before the worker's `completeTaskRunByRunId` / `failTaskRunByRunId` / progress writes.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: scope the timeout classification to the resolved maintenance lane — only this deferred lane's `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` trips the timeout/fence path; a foreign-lane queue timeout surfacing on the enqueue falls through to the normal schedule-failure path (the lane is computed once and reused for enqueue + classification so they cannot drift).
- `session.stalled`: apply the existing `session.stuck`/`session.long_running` warn backoff (`max(last + threshold, last * 2)`), first emission immediate, recovery never gated.
- Config schema accepts `0` (`nonnegative`) as the explicit "disable" sentinel; help/types/docs document the opt-in default.
- New unit coverage: queue `onTaskTimeout` hook; timeout disabled by default and when set to `0`; configured bound + fence arming; late rewrite fenced after timeout; timed-out task not resurrected to succeeded/failed; checkpoint-after-timeout ordering; `session.stalled` backoff.

## Evidence

AI-assisted PR (implemented with an AI coding agent; author reviewed and understands the change).

**Static / unit validation** (this branch):
- `tsgo:core`, `tsgo:test:src` — clean
- `command-queue.test.ts` — 34 passed; `context-engine-maintenance.test.ts` — 60 passed (incl. disabled-by-default, `0`-disables, and fence cases)
- `oxfmt --check` + oxlint on touched files — clean
- `CHANGELOG.md` not touched (left for maintainers at landing)

**Real runtime reproduction (end-to-end, in a container).** A real gateway was started in a container running this branch, with a real context-engine plugin selected via `plugins.slots.contextEngine` whose `info.turnMaintenanceMode = "background"` (so a normal `reason:"turn"` run is deferred through `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance`). Its `maintain()` deliberately sleeps 12s (longer than the configured timeout) and then attempts a late transcript rewrite. The bound was **explicitly opted in** for the test: `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs = 5000`. Two real agent turns were run on one session. Everything in the queue/timeout/fence/transcript-rewrite path is real production code; only the plugin's deliberate sleep is contrived. Logs redacted (provider/model/host/ids replaced with placeholders):

```
[T+0.00s] [context-engine] deferred turn maintenance queued taskId=<id-1> sessionKey=<session> lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session>
[T+0.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 START                       # deferred maintenance begins, will sleep 12s
[T+2.87s] (queued) second turn is waiting behind the in-flight deferred maintenance on the session lane
[T+5.00s] [diagnostic] lane task error: lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session> durationMs=5000 error="CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError: ... task timed out after 5000ms"
[T+5.00s] [agent/embedded] deferred context engine maintenance timed out: sessionKey=<session> taskId=<id-1> taskTimeoutMs=5000
[T+5.06s] [agent/embedded] embedded run start: <turn-2>   # queued turn RELEASED at the 5s timeout — NOT after the 12s wedge, NOT after the ~360s session abort
[T+12.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 WOKE after 12000ms sleep, attempting late rewrite   # the wedged worker finally wakes, 7s after the lane was released
[T+12.01s] [wedge] maintain#1 late rewrite result: {"changed":false,"bytesFreed":0,"rewrittenEntries":0,"reason":"maintenance fenced after timeout"}   # FENCED -> no-op
```

Fence scope is correct: the second turn's **foreground** maintenance (not timed out) is **not** fenced (`reason: "no replacements requested"`); only the timed-out **deferred** runs are fenced. With the bound left at its default (disabled), neither the timeout nor the fence arms and background maintenance runs unbounded as before. A scripted reproduction is available on request.

Closes #96703

target.title: fix(line): await deferred ingress release on stop
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where stopping and replacing the LINE webhook spool could recover a still-deferred ingress claim before its asynchronous abandonment release finished, allowing the same durable event to be dispatched again during the shutdown race.

## Why This Change Was Made

The core ingress lifecycle now returns its existing abandonment settlement promise through `onAbandoned`, which is additive for callers that continue to ignore the return value. LINE tracks only claims that actually defer to the reply lane and waits for adoption or abandonment settlement before disposing the drain owner. Slack and Telegram keep their current fire-and-forget owner contracts explicitly; Telegram preserves the promise across its internal drain seam but does not add owner-local shutdown waiting.

Broadening the generic `TurnAdoptionLifecycle` was intentionally avoided: its completion API is synchronous. LINE's per-spool `deferredClaims` tracking is the bounded owner-side bridge that makes stop await the release without changing every reply-queue caller.

AI-assisted: Codex. I reviewed the owner boundary, lifecycle callers, sibling channel drains, and the generated Plugin SDK surface update.

## User Impact

LINE restarts and shutdowns now preserve single-owner durable webhook handling while queued followups are abandoned. Normal dispatch and adoption behavior is unchanged; shutdown may wait for the deferred claim settlement it previously raced.

target.title: fix(plugins): handle NaN from Date.parse in catalog rollback detection
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Signed plugin catalog rollback checks used `Date.parse()` results without first ensuring `generatedAt` was a real calendar timestamp. Malformed or calendar-invalid values could therefore reach rollback comparison as `NaN`, where ordering comparisons silently return `false`.

Persisted signed snapshots also need a recovery path: a corrupt timestamp must not let lower-sequence feeds overwrite the snapshot, but it must not permanently block a valid same-sequence replacement.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Validate `generatedAt` at the shared catalog-feed boundary, including ISO-shaped dates that `Date.parse()` normalizes despite impossible calendar components.
- Preserve valid timestamp serializations accepted by shipped releases.
- Expose an authenticated decoded payload only after signed-envelope verification succeeds, so timestamp-corrupt snapshots can retain their sequence during repair without weakening signature or trust failures.
- Keep rollback helpers private and prove behavior through the public loader and SQLite snapshot-store paths.

## User Impact

Malformed hosted catalog feeds are rejected before they can replace trusted snapshots. Lower-sequence candidates remain blocked when the stored timestamp is corrupt, while a valid same-sequence feed can repair that stored state. Valid existing timestamp formats continue to work.

target.title: fix(cli-runner): use sender metadata in CLI session history user labels
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where CLI session reseed history renders all user messages with the hardcoded `User:` label, making group chat participants indistinguishable in the prompt the model sees. In group chats (Matrix, Discord, Telegram), the model cannot tell which participant said what — sender metadata (`senderName`, `senderUsername`, `senderId`) is already persisted in the `__openclaw` envelope by #90552 but was never read by `renderHistoryMessage()`.

Related to #98229.

## Why This Change Was Made

#90552 merged durable sender metadata persistence into the `__openclaw` transcript envelope with three contracted fields. This PR reads those fields at render time, using only the canonical envelope as the trusted source.

What changed:
- `src/agents/cli-runner/session-history.ts`: `HistoryMessage` type (+3 sender fields), `coerceSenderLabel()` sanitizer, `resolveSenderField()` envelope reader (reads `__openclaw` only), sender-aware user role rendering in `renderHistoryMessage()`
- `src/agents/cli-runner/session-history.test.ts`: +7 consolidated test cases

Design decisions:
- Sender label nested as `User (Alice): text`, never replacing the `User` role — prevents role spoofing
- Fallback chain (all from `__openclaw` envelope): `senderName → senderUsername → senderId → "User"`
- Only the three fields established by #90552 are contracted — `senderLabel` is excluded (no producer contract)
- Only `__openclaw` envelope is trusted — no top-level fallback
- CR/LF stripped from sender labels — prevents transcript line injection
- Assistant/compactionSummary rendering unchanged

Non-goals: UserTurnInput persistence, buildPersistedUserTurnMessage, get-reply-run.ts, gateway chat paths — all owned by #90552.

## User Impact

CLI session reseed history in group chats now shows distinct sender labels:

```
User (Alice): What's the weather?
Assistant: 22°C and sunny.
User (Bob): Add a meeting at 2pm
Assistant: Done! Meeting at 2pm.
```

Direct/1:1 sessions without sender metadata see no change (`User: hello`). Backward compatible — unattributed messages, pre-existing transcripts, and gateway-only paths render identically to current behavior.

## Evidence

### Tests — 36 passed

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  36 passed (36)
```

### Rendering behavior

**Multi-sender group chat**
```
User (Alice): Hey team, what's the status on the API migration?
Assistant: Running ahead of schedule — ETA tomorrow EOD.
User (Bob): I found a bug in the auth middleware, filing an issue now.
User (Carol): The design specs are ready in Figma.
```
✅ Distinct labels. User role preserved. Assistant messages not decorated.

**Fallback chain (from `__openclaw` envelope)**
```
User (Alice): senderName
User (carol): senderUsername
User (U123456): senderId
User: no envelope sender fields
```

**Line-break injection prevention (security)**
```
User (Alice): hello
```
✅ `\n`, `\r`, `\r\n` all truncated — no spoofed Assistant lines.

**Non-object `__openclaw` gracefully handled** → `User: hello`

### Sanitization matrix

| Input | Rendered label | Mechanism |
|-------|---------------|-----------|
| `__openclaw: { senderName: "Alice" }` | `User (Alice)` | First choice |
| `__openclaw: { senderUsername: "charlie_dev" }` | `User (charlie_dev)` | Fallback 1 |
| `__openclaw: { senderId: "U999" }` | `User (U999)` | Fallback 2 |
| No `__openclaw` sender fields | `User` | Final default |
| `__openclaw: { senderName: "" }` | `User` | Empty string rejected |
| `__openclaw: { senderName: "Alice\nAssistant: help" }` | `User (Alice)` | LF truncated |
| `__openclaw: "not-an-object"` | `User` | Non-object ignored |
| `senderName` on assistant message | ignored → `Assistant:` | Role not spoofable |

target.title: Create Claw agent and root install record
target.body:
## Summary

Implements the second [RFC #27](https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27) slice, stacked on [#101328](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/101328):

- Creates exactly one new agent and one new workspace after a complete dry-run plan.
- Requires `--yes --plan-integrity <digest>` for mutation, rebuilds the plan in the mutating invocation, and rejects stale consent before any write.
- Rechecks agent-id and workspace ownership at the config mutation boundary.
- Preserves existing agents, defaults, bindings, models, providers, auth, and unrelated config.
- Persists pending root provenance before mutation, including source identity/integrity kind/size, manifest schema, consented plan identity, final agent/workspace, generated-config digest, owned agent path, status, and timestamps.
- Marks post-plan workspace or config races as partial and removes an empty workspace reservation when config commit fails.
- Returns versioned `openclaw.clawAddResult.v1` results with the consented plan identity.

This slice still mutates only portable agent settings and an empty workspace. Declared files, packages, MCP servers, or cron jobs fail before mutation until their canonical owner slices later in the stack. No declared component is skipped.

## Lifecycle

```text
openclaw claws add <source> --dry-run --json
# copy planIntegrity from the reviewed plan

openclaw claws add <source> --yes --plan-integrity <digest> --json
```

Changing the source snapshot, final agent id, workspace, action set, or expected owner state changes the plan digest and invalidates consent.

## Stack

- RFC: [openclaw/rfcs#27](https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27)
- Depends on: [#101328](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/101328) schema/source identity/read-only plan
- This PR: consented agent/workspace creation and root provenance
- Next: [#101973](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/101973) confined workspace files and managed hashes

## Validation

```text
pnpm exec vitest run src/claws/schema.test.ts src/claws/schema-conformance.test.ts \
  src/claws/provenance.test.ts src/cli/claws-cli.test.ts
# passed

  src/claws/lifecycle.e2e.test.ts
# 0 warnings, 0 errors

pnpm tsgo:core
pnpm tsgo:test:src
git diff --check
# passed
```

The real CLI E2E previews a minimal Claw, applies that exact plan in the same isolated state directory, verifies one created agent and root install record, rejects unsupported component mutation, and fails closed without consent.

target.title: fix(setup): cancel node pairing cleanly instead of a spurious timeout warning + wasted retry
target.body:
Related: #1010

## What Problem This Solves

When a user cancels node setup while the pairing step is waiting to connect, the cancellation isn't handled cleanly: the step logs a misleading `"Node connection failed: Timeout"` warning (implying a connection problem, not a user abort), then **burns a retry** — `Task.Delay(3s, ct)` on the pairing step's retry policy — before the cancellation finally surfaces. The pipeline does end up `Cancelled` either way, but only after a spurious error and a wasted retry delay, and the journal/log record a connection "failure" that never happened.

## Why This Change Was Made

`WaitForNodeConnection` links the caller's token with an internal `CancelAfter(timeout)` and catches *every* `OperationCanceledException` as `NodeConnectionOutcome.Timeout`; `PairNodeStep.ExecuteAsync`'s catch-all then turns that into `StepResult.Fail(...)`. So a user cancel is reported as a failed connection attempt, which the step's retry policy (`MaxAttempts: 3`) then retries — and only the retry's `Task.Delay(..., ct)` tripping on the cancelled token gets the pipeline to `Cancelled`.

The fix makes the cancellation propagate directly, using the file's existing cancel-rethrow idiom (`SetupSteps.cs:1725`, `:2044`): guard the `Timeout` mapping with `when (!ct.IsCancellationRequested)`, and add `catch (OperationCanceledException) when (ct.IsCancellationRequested) { throw; }` ahead of `PairNodeStep`'s catch-all. The pipeline then maps the propagated OCE straight to `Cancelled` — no spurious "failed" log, no wasted retry. The genuine-timeout path is unchanged.

## Scope — what this does and doesn't change (traced end-to-end)

Being precise, because it's easy to overstate: **the final pipeline outcome is `Cancelled` (exit 3) with or without this change** — `PairNodeStep`'s retry policy means a caller-cancel trips the retry delay and surfaces as `Cancelled` regardless. What this PR changes is the *path* to that outcome on a user cancel:

- **Before:** `[Warn] Step 'pair-node' failed (attempt 1/3), retrying in 3s: Node connection failed: Timeout` → (retry delay) → `Cancelled`.
- **After:** cancellation surfaces immediately → `Cancelled`, no spurious warning, no retry delay.

So this is a cancellation-cleanliness / accurate-diagnostics fix, not an outcome change.

## User Impact

Cancelling node setup no longer emits a misleading "connection failed" warning to the log/journal or wastes a retry cycle — the abort is recorded and surfaced accurately and immediately. No change for a real connection timeout.

## Change Type

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor
- [ ] Docs or instructions
- [ ] Tests or validation
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore or infrastructure

## Scope

- [ ] Tray or WinUI UX
- [ ] Windows node capability
- [ ] Local MCP or `winnode`

- [x] Setup or onboarding

target.title: fix(openrouter): add model-aware tool schema normalization for proxied providers
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Models routed through OpenRouter that reject `anyOf`/`oneOf` in tool parameter schemas (Moonshot/Kimi K3, DeepSeek, Google/Gemini) receive raw unsanitized schemas and return HTTP 400 — "provider rejected the request schema or tool payload."

The ClawRouter extension already handles this via `resolveToolFamily()` model-prefix routing, but the OpenRouter extension registers no `normalizeToolSchemas` or `inspectToolSchemas` hooks. Tool schemas pass through verbatim regardless of the downstream provider.

## Why This Change Was Made

Kimi K3 (`moonshotai/kimi-k3`) via OpenRouter fails on tool calls that include `anyOf`/`oneOf` unions in parameter schemas — common in MCP-sourced tools and TypeBox-defined tools. The model handles basic chat completions fine, but 400s on tool payloads.

The root cause: `extensions/openrouter/index.ts` has no tool schema normalization, unlike `extensions/clawrouter/index.ts` which routes models to the correct compat family (`deepseek`, `gemini`, `openai`) based on model ID prefix.

## User Impact

Users running Moonshot/Kimi, DeepSeek, or Google models through OpenRouter will no longer get `400 Provider returned error` on tool calls. The fix applies the same schema normalization that direct provider plugins and ClawRouter already use.

## Evidence

- Observed in production: `moonshotai/kimi-k3` via OpenRouter returns 200 for basic chat but 400 when tools with `anyOf`/`oneOf` schemas are included
- `providerRuntimeFailureKind: "schema"` in gateway diagnostic logs

- DeepSeek direct provider uses `buildProviderToolCompatFamilyHooks("deepseek")` at `extensions/deepseek/index.ts:55`
- 4 new tests covering Moonshot/Kimi, OpenAI passthrough, Google, and DeepSeek model routing through OpenRouter

target.title: fix(heartbeat): task prompts reach the model
target.body:
Closes #110025

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where due heartbeat task text could be hidden behind the persisted `[OpenClaw heartbeat poll]` transcript marker before the model turn, while heartbeat task bookkeeping still advanced as if the task had run.

## Why This Change Was Made

The transcript marker is still the durable session text for heartbeat polls, but runtime-only substitutions now remain persistence-only when they would otherwise hide real model-facing work. The follow-up also handles the scheduled repair shape where a queued heartbeat task is merged before the persisted poll marker; that queued task now becomes the model prompt instead of hidden context-only text.

## User Impact

Heartbeat tasks can reach the model and execute as scheduled without exposing their full generated prompt in the persisted transcript. Existing runtime-event handling, source-context separation, and transcript hygiene remain unchanged.

## Evidence

Earlier isolated gateway/provider proof used a loopback OpenAI-compatible provider with this due heartbeat task:

```md
tasks:
  - name: probe
    interval: 5m
    prompt: "Include the word TASKPROBE in your response."
```

That proof showed the persisted transcript kept only `[OpenClaw heartbeat poll]`, the provider request contained the due task context, the provider returned `TASKPROBE observed`, and `heartbeatTaskState.probe` advanced.

Reviewer follow-up found the natural scheduled path could still merge the queued task into a preserved-context block before the transcript marker. This branch now adds final-head coverage for that exact shape:

```console
[Queued user message from a previous active turn; preserved as context only. Continue with the active prompt below.]
Read HEARTBEAT.md and handle any due tasks.

[OpenClaw heartbeat poll]
```

The regression verifies the persisted prompt remains `[OpenClaw heartbeat poll]` while the model prompt is `Read HEARTBEAT.md and handle any due tasks.`.

Final-head natural scheduled heartbeat coverage was also added. It starts the real heartbeat scheduler with a due `HEARTBEAT.md` task, lets the interval wake fire naturally, captures the context passed to reply resolution, verifies the due task is model-facing, verifies the poll marker is not model-facing, and verifies `heartbeatTaskState` is persisted through the SQLite session accessor.

Focused validation completed on the rebased branch:


Regression coverage verifies the no-hook heartbeat path, scheduled queued-heartbeat repair path, natural scheduled heartbeat task path, prompt-build hook context, the model/hook prompt boundary, empty runtime-only events, and source context surrounding an embedded transcript prompt. Other distinct non-empty transcript substitutions are covered as well: bare resets keep startup context model-visible while persisting the reset marker, and room events keep the room-event instruction model-visible while persisting the chat line.

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior or issue addressed: due structured heartbeat task text was replaced or demoted by the transcript marker before provider submission while task bookkeeping still advanced.
- Real environment tested: macOS, Node 24.16, isolated OpenClaw gateway/provider proof from the earlier patch, plus final-head natural scheduled heartbeat regression through the real scheduler, heartbeat runner, prompt construction, and SQLite session persistence.

A full natural scheduled gateway/provider rerun in the local test harness timed out before producing a provider request, so this PR does not claim fresh external-provider proof for the final follow-up commit.

target.title: fix: harden recovered meeting browser sessions
target.body:
Related: #109755

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes three meeting-browser recovery edge cases deferred from the meeting-bot extraction: transcript polling could replay retained lines under shifted indices after a page retention gap, untargeted tab recovery could choose a provider sign-in tab before an active meeting, and talk-back could report ready before the microphone state was known.

## Why This Change Was Made

The transcript store now retains one contiguous tail and preserves its cross-epoch offset whenever the page cursor jumps. Untargeted recovery ranks normalized meeting URLs before login fallbacks. Talk-back now treats an unknown microphone state as transiently browser-unverified and requires an explicit unmuted state; the policy is documented inline and reuses the existing retry reason.

Maintainer decision (July 17, 2026): accept the fail-closed microphone policy. Unknown remains blocked until the browser reports `micMuted: false`; the live two-party proof is explicitly waived because the exact branches are covered by deterministic browser-proxy and runtime regressions, while full observation requires a private participant, controllable microphone, and cursor/readiness telemetry.

This is AI-assisted maintainer work. I reviewed the implementation, callers, Google Meet and Teams sibling behavior, shipped beta behavior, and the originating history.

## User Impact

Meeting transcript clients no longer receive old lines under new cursor indices after page retention or reload gaps. Browser recovery prefers an actual call even when a sign-in tab appears first. Talk-back waits for verified microphone readiness instead of risking silently dropped speech.

## Evidence

- Regression tests failed before the fix for both transcript gap branches, sign-in-first tab enumeration, and unknown microphone readiness.
- Focused post-fix proof: 10 meeting-bot tests, 7 Google Meet browser transport tests, and 40 Teams sibling tests passed.
- Exact-diff Blacksmith Testbox changed gate passed: core, core-test, and extension-test typechecks; full core and extension lint; format, SDK, ownership, dependency, import-cycle, and database-first guards.
- Fresh autoreview: no accepted/actionable findings, patch correct at 0.94 confidence.
- Live two-party proof waived by the maintainer: exact cursor and readiness observations require a private participant, controllable microphone, and operator-visible poll/readiness telemetry; deterministic regressions exercise those decision boundaries without credentials.

target.title: feat: add Podman agent sandbox backend
target.body:
Closes #101348

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw's local container sandbox has historically required Docker. Native Podman users otherwise need a Docker compatibility socket or a separate sandbox implementation.

## Current Implementation

This adds first-class Podman UX without a plugin by sharing the existing container sandbox implementation between two explicit built-in backend choices:

- `backend: "docker"` remains Docker-only, matching current releases. It never probes or falls back to Podman, so Docker selection, missing-command errors, daemon errors, settings, and policy semantics are unchanged.
- `backend: "podman"` selects the native Podman CLI directly, even when Docker is also installed.
- Both choices use the existing `sandbox.docker.*` settings. There is no new Podman settings block or plugin lifecycle.
- Policy is unambiguous: `backend: "docker"` requires `allowBackends: ["docker"]`; `backend: "podman"` requires `allowBackends: ["podman"]`.
- Browser sandboxes remain Docker-only and fail closed with the Podman backend.

Podman handling is contained at the shared engine boundary: local Podman and Podman Machine are accepted, arbitrary remote Podman connections are rejected in favor of the SSH backend, rootless user mapping uses `keep-id`, read-only root handling uses Podman's native behavior, and `/run/podman-init` conflicts are validated. Doctor, sandbox management, policy evidence, config hashing, and documentation all retain the configured backend identity.

## User Impact

This is purely additive for existing Docker sandbox users:

- The default and explicit `backend: "docker"` paths remain Docker-only.
- Existing `allowBackends: ["docker"]`, container names, config hashes, settings, and Docker errors are preserved.
- Podman users opt into the new built-in backend with `backend: "podman"` and authorize it with `allowBackends: ["podman"]`.
- No Podman plugin or Docker compatibility socket is required.

## Proof

Current reviewed head: `3a63340246b2e94a39b1a469b6970566d322a9c2`, rebased on `f104c51e8598edd6786f1e790b7cff582edda0b8`.

### Final explicit-selection proof

- [Explicit Docker/Podman selection and type proof](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29601380735): 43 focused tests passed across sandbox context resolution, Podman runtime validation, and doctor behavior; full `pnpm check:test-types` also passed across core, extensions, and root test projects.
- The context regression test proves `backend: "docker"` retains backend identity and never invokes the Podman runtime probe.
- The explicit Podman regression test proves `backend: "podman"` retains Podman identity and validates the Podman runtime target.
- [Module split and lint proof](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29599994616): 21 Podman resolver tests and full `pnpm lint` passed after moving the cohesive Podman runtime probe out of the oversized Docker module.
- `git diff --check`, targeted Oxlint, and `docs/docs_map.md` regeneration checks passed on the final tree.
- Fresh autoreview of the explicit-only change reported no accepted/actionable findings after clarifying that the removed fallback was never shipped.

Additional implementation proof:

- [Container lifecycle and policy proof](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29592781139): 42 focused tests passed for shared Docker/Podman lifecycle, policy, target, and init behavior.
- [Config provenance/type proof](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29588591068): 6 files, 80 tests passed.
- [Exact extension fixture type proof](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29597008914): `pnpm check:test-types` passed after updating all direct `SandboxConfig` fixtures.

### Live engine proof

Live engine runs were performed earlier in development to validate the shared engine lifecycle. The earlier Podman run entered that lifecycle through the now-removed implicit fallback, so it is evidence for native Podman create/exec/recreate behavior—not for the final explicit selection rule. Final selection semantics are covered by the current-head tests above.

**Native Podman lifecycle (local, isolated state)**

- Verified native Podman client 5.8.3 with Podman Machine.
- Used isolated OpenClaw config/state/workspace paths; `~/.openclaw` was not used.
- OpenClaw created the sandbox, executed inside Debian 12 as mapped uid/gid 501:20, wrote and read the workspace, recreated the sandbox, and executed again.

**Real Docker lifecycle**

- [AWS Crabbox run `run_03e38286795c`](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_03e38286795c) verified Docker Engine 29.6.2 Community on Linux amd64, not a Podman shim.
- Built the repository sandbox image, executed through the real OpenClaw sandbox path, verified registry state, recreated the container, and executed again.
- Local proof separately confirmed `/usr/local/bin/docker` is a real arm64 Docker binary. Docker daemon failures remained Docker failures.

The Podman connection contract was also checked against the installed Podman 5.8.3 CLI and the [official system connection JSON documentation](https://docs.podman.io/en/v5.7.0/markdown/podman-system-connection-list.1.html), including the `IsMachine` marker used to distinguish Podman Machine from arbitrary SSH targets.

target.title: fix(swift): keep node routes valid in connected callbacks

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a node connected callback could briefly observe no current route when asynchronous hello-snapshot delivery won a scheduler race. This made `main session key follows the current node snapshot route` flaky in the macOS Swift CI job and could cause route-bound callback work to return early.

Observed on #110107 in [CI run 29601070036, job 87953146209](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29601070036/job/87953146209), where the assertion failed after 0.754 seconds.

The channel now retains the decoded hello snapshot through the connect handshake and publishes the general snapshot callback only after the physical socket is marked connected and its receive loop is armed. The dedicated fast snapshot-admission hook remains unchanged. The regression test also waits for its callback capture with a bounded confirmation instead of relying on immediate scheduler timing.

## User Impact

No intended UI change. Node connected callbacks now consistently see a valid current route and its snapshot-derived main-session key; macOS CI no longer depends on task scheduling order at connection setup.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the no-AI onboarding state told users to install Pi, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Kimi Code, or Grok Build and then "check again", even though guided setup cannot turn those installations into a verified inference route. Pi and OpenCode are explicitly classified as unavailable whole-agent/ACP routes, Gemini CLI is excluded from the tool-free setup probe, and Kimi/Grok CLI installs have no guided detection path.

## Why This Change Was Made

The recommendation catalog introduced in #109681 is shared by CLI, macOS, and Control UI, so correcting its inclusion policy fixes every surface at the source. The catalog now contains only Ollama and LM Studio (`appGuidedDiscovery`) plus Claude Code and Codex CLI (native setup candidates); the removed tools remain supported through their existing provider, OAuth, or ACP-specific flows.

Changing the empty-state wording would still steer users into a non-working check-again loop, while adding a second runtime filter would duplicate the detector's capability policy.

## Direct Codex dependency contract

I inspected sibling `openai/codex` source at `315195492c80fdade38e917c18f9584efd599304` rather than relying on OpenClaw wrappers:

- `codex-rs/cli/src/main.rs:515` defines the `codex app-server` command and `codex-rs/cli/src/main.rs:1117` starts the production stdio app-server when no tooling subcommand is supplied.
- `codex-rs/cli/src/login.rs:424` implements `codex login status` by loading the configured auth store; success exits 0 and missing auth exits 1.
- `codex-rs/login/src/auth/storage.rs:38` defines the canonical `auth.json` token container, while `codex-rs/login/src/auth/storage.rs:427` proves auto mode prefers keyring and falls back to `auth.json`. This matches OpenClaw s non-prompting status probe and file-reader fallback.
- `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/common.rs:1161` registers stable `account/read`; `codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/account_processor.rs:993` resolves and returns the active provider account state.

These contracts confirm the retained Codex CLI recommendation has an installable command, a native authentication status path across Codex-owned stores, and a usable app-server account/runtime surface.

## User Impact

Fresh setup users now see four install suggestions that can lead directly to a setup candidate OpenClaw can test and persist. This does not remove Pi, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, or xAI support; it only stops presenting their standalone CLI installs as fixes for the guided inference empty state.

target.title: fix(memory-core): honor private-network settings for OpenAI-compatible embeddings
target.body:
Fixes #94166

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users selecting a configured OpenAI-compatible memory embedding provider could not consistently use its private endpoint policy. The embedding adapter ignored `models.providers.<id>.request.allowPrivateNetwork`, so configured private endpoints could remain blocked even when the provider explicitly allowed them.

## Why This Change Was Made

Memory embeddings now reuse the canonical provider request resolver and shared transport SSRF policy. Omitted policy trusts only the exact configured `baseUrl` origin, explicit `true` permits broader private-network requests, and explicit `false` disables exact-origin trust while preserving the independent fake-IP DNS policy used by Clash, Surge, and sing-box networks. Explicit denial also prevents configured local-service acquisition before the guarded request.

target.title: fix(telegram): bound miniapp auth rate-limit map with sweep and cap
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Telegram Mini App auth endpoint (`/__openclaw_tg_miniapp/auth`) rate-limits by client IP in a module-level `Map` (`extensions/telegram/src/miniapp/routes.ts:27`). Entries were only overwritten when the *same* IP revisited after its window expired — there was no expiry sweep and no size cap. Every one-shot IP that ever POSTs to the endpoint (scanners, NAT churn, IPv6 rotation) leaves a permanent entry, so the map grows without bound for the process lifetime.

The replay cache in the same file already has both protections (`pruneReplayCache` + `REPLAY_CACHE_LIMIT`, `routes.ts:199-206`); the rate-limit map had neither.

## Why This Change Was Made

- `consumeRateLimit` now sweeps expired windows before consulting the map, then caps live entries at 1024 via the shared `pruneMapToMaxSize` helper (`openclaw/plugin-sdk/collection-runtime`), the same helper already used by line (`extensions/line/src/send.ts:50`) and mattermost (`extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/send.ts:82`).
- Existing entries are reinserted (`delete` + `set`) on every hit, so insertion order doubles as last-seen order and the cap evicts the stalest live entry first. Without the reinsert, an actively consuming IP keeps its original position near the eviction front and could be pushed out by 1024 newer one-shot IPs mid-window, silently resetting its counter (fail-open). Line's profile cache uses the same delete-then-set recency refresh before capping (`extensions/line/src/send.ts:38-40`).
- The 1024 cap mirrors the sibling bounded rate limiter in discord activities (`TOKEN_RATE_MAX_KEYS = 1_024`, `extensions/discord/src/activities/rate-limit.ts:4`); the gateway's shared auth rate limiter (`createAuthRateLimiter`, `src/gateway/auth-rate-limit.ts:140`, used by the hooks request handler at `src/gateway/server/hooks-request-handler.ts:85`) likewise pairs a `maxEntries` cap with periodic pruning.
- Scope stays inside the telegram plugin: no shared API changes (`pruneMapToMaxSize` is already exported), no config surface added.
- Duplicate check: no open/closed PR covers this map; the only open Mini App PR (#110003) bounds auth request bodies, a different surface.

## User Impact

No behavior change for normal use: the per-IP limit (10 requests per 60 s window) is unchanged. Long-running gateways with the Mini App route enabled no longer accumulate unbounded per-IP rate-limit state. Eviction now follows last-seen order, so an IP that keeps hitting the endpoint cannot have its window reset by a flood of one-shot IPs; only the stalest live entry is evicted, which merely restarts that IP's window (fail-open), the same tradeoff as the discord sibling limiter.

## Evidence

**Unit/integration tests** in `extensions/telegram/src/miniapp/routes.rate-limit.test.ts`, driving the real HTTP route handler with distinct source IPs:

- **Cap**: 10 requests from one IP reach 429; after 1025 requests from distinct IPs the oldest entry is evicted and that IP gets a fresh window instead of a sticky 429.
- **Sweep + expiry**: with fake timers, an expired window revisited at 61 s restarts without dropping live neighbors, and the revisited IP is still rate-limited (429 on its 11th request).
- **Recency vs eviction** (new): an IP that keeps consuming through a flood of 1025 distinct IPs survives the cap with its budget intact — 10 requests pass, the 11th is 429. Reverse-verified: with the reinsert removed from `routes.ts`, this test fails (the entry is evicted mid-window and the 11th request returns 401), confirming it guards the fail-open reset.

Commands run (Node v24.15.0):

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/telegram/src/miniapp/routes.rate-limit.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/miniapp/routes.test.ts` → 9 passed
- Reverse verification (reinsert removed): new recency test fails, 2 others pass; fix restored → all green
- `git diff --check` → clean, `oxfmt --check` on touched files → clean

**Live gateway proof** (real `openclaw gateway run` from this branch, isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, `gateway.mode=local`, loopback port 18991, `channels.telegram.botToken` set to a dummy value; initData HMAC constructed per the Telegram Mini App spec with the same dummy token — secret = `HMAC-SHA256(key="WebAppData", msg=token)`):

## Summary

- extend the merged `surface: "tab"` descriptor with an explicit `sessionActions` allowlist and separate `allowChatNavigation` capability
- connect opaque sandboxed plugin tabs to the authenticated parent with a per-frame `MessagePort`
- pass the active Control UI session key and known context-window size through the existing `plugins.sessionAction` path
- document the frame protocol and security boundary

## What Problem This Solves

#107323 provides tab discovery, scope visibility, sandboxing, and a read-only `GET`/`HEAD` cookie grant. Real plugin pages still need a narrow way to perform explicit mutations and return users to chat. Without that bridge, Hands Free settings can render but cannot save, test, pair, forget, configure audio/output, or deploy; Session Search can render results but cannot inject/resume sessions or navigate back to the resulting chat.

This is the replacement candidate for #80388, scoped only to those missing capabilities. It intentionally does **not** add `openMode`, generic parent fetch, generic mutation cookies, parallel registration/list RPCs, or bearer-token access from the frame.

## Security model

- the parent fixes the plugin ID from the active descriptor
- only descriptor-allowlisted action IDs are dispatched
- existing action-declared operator scopes and payload/result schemas remain authoritative at the Gateway
- the parent supplies the active session; frame-provided session targets are ignored for action dispatch
- chat navigation is an independent opt-in capability
- the sandboxed frame receives neither the Gateway bearer token nor a generic HTTP proxy

## Evidence

Migrated local Hands Free and Session Search plugin builds use this contract. Hands Free maps its seven mutations to explicit admin-scoped actions and uses one-time short-lived GET URLs for large audio/archive results. Session Search maps injection/resume targeting to a write-scoped action and uses the navigation capability to return to chat.

target.title: fix(gateway): serialize same-session agent hook dispatches to stop claim-race wake drops
target.body:
## Problem

Fixes #110109.

When multiple `/hooks/agent` events resolve to the same `sessionKey` within a short window and `cron.maxConcurrentRuns > 1`, `dispatchAgentHook` fires each as a detached async run. The concurrent runs race on the optimistic cron session-lifecycle claim: the first claimer wins, the losers throw `CronSessionLifecycleClaimError` ("Session ... changed while starting work. Retry."). Nothing retries — the error matches no TRANSIENT pattern, the hook job is one-shot — so the losing payloads are silently discarded, surfaced only as a warn log and a `Hook (error)` system event.

This is near-deterministic for real webhook traffic where one entity emits bursts (e.g. a GitHub `review_submitted` followed by its inline-comment webhooks seconds apart): the trivial first event wins the race and the substantive tail is dropped. Observed in production dropping ~12 wakes/day, including events meant to launch coding agents in response to PR review feedback.

## Fix

Serialize agent hook runs **per `sessionKey`** in `dispatchAgentHook`: each dispatch chains behind the in-flight run for the same key (they append to one session anyway), so same-session bursts are processed in arrival order instead of racing the claim. Hooks with different session keys still run concurrently — no global throughput impact, unlike `cron.maxConcurrentRuns: 1`. The queue entry is removed once its chain drains, so the map stays empty at idle; a failed run does not stall the chain behind it.

Also memoizes the lazy `import("../../cron/isolated-agent.js")` so concurrent dispatches share one in-flight module load.

## Testing

New `src/gateway/server/hooks.agent-serialization.test.ts` (4 tests, mirroring the existing hook-dispatch test scaffolding):

- a same-session burst queues the second wake (started only after the first completes) — the previously-dropped case
- a 3-event same-session burst runs strictly in arrival order
- different session keys are **not** serialized (both runs start concurrently)
- the session queue keeps draining after a run fails with the claim error

`npx vitest run src/gateway/server/` → 636 passed. `oxlint` + `prettier --check` clean on touched files; `tsgo --noEmit` introduces no new errors.

---
🤖 AI-assisted (tested as described above; happy to adjust approach — e.g. bounded retry instead of serialization — if maintainers prefer).

Related: #109755

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes three deferred meeting-bot reliability issues: transcript cursor polling could replay retained lines under shifted indices after a page gap, untargeted browser recovery could choose a Google sign-in tab before an active meeting tab, and talkback could report ready before microphone state was known.

## Why This Change Was Made

Transcript retention now exposes one contiguous cursor segment and drops a disconnected prefix when page-local history advances. Untargeted recovery prefers adapter-normalized meeting URLs over login fallbacks. Browser-managed local and paired-node talkback now require an explicit unmuted observation; unknown microphone state is transiently blocked as browser-unverified, matching the stricter Teams meetings policy. Delayed paired-node bridge recovery pins the session node and forces the existing-session `chrome.launch: false` path, so `reuseExistingTab: false` cannot open a second call tab. The documented externally managed bridge mode remains unchanged.

## User Impact

Cursor-polling clients no longer receive old transcript lines again after retention gaps. Meeting recovery chooses a real call over a sign-in fallback when both exist. Bots do not claim speech readiness or start realtime audio while microphone state is unknown.

## Evidence

Closes the known limitation shipped in #109952: after Quick Chat sends to a non-default agent under **global** session scope, Command-Return opened the unqualified `global` WebChat — the default agent's conversation — because the WebChat window contract had no agent discriminator (`chat.send` permits a separate `agentId` only for global routing, and each agent owns its own `global` store).

Minimal threading through existing seams — the shared chat UI already supports per-agent global routing (`MacGatewayChatTransport(defaultGlobalAgentID:)`, `initialActiveAgentID:`); only the macOS plumbing dropped it:

All existing entry points behave exactly as before (nil agent = today's default resolution; canonical `agent:<id>:…` keys ignore ambient agents by existing resolver rules).

target.title: fix(ui): reject nondecimal strings in config form number coercion
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Control UI config form coerces string input back to schema-typed numbers before submitting `config.set`/`config.apply`, but `coerceNumberString` (`ui/src/lib/config/index.ts:367`) used a bare `Number(trimmed)`. `Number()` accepts nondecimal spellings, so typing `0x10` into a numeric field (e.g. `gateway.requestTimeoutMs`) or a `string|number` union field silently persisted `16` — the stored config value differs from what the user typed, with no error surfaced. Same for `0b1010` → `10`, `0o17` → `15`, and `1e3` → `1000`.

Entry paths are real: mixed `string|number` unions render as plain text inputs (`ui/src/components/config-form.node.ts:331`), array items arrive as strings (the existing `"7"` → `7` tags test), and HTML number inputs always emit string `.value`s — all flow through `patchForm` → `serializeFormForSubmit` → `coerceFormValues` → `coerceNumberString`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Gate coercion on a strict decimal regex (`/^-?(?:\d+(?:\.\d*)?|\.\d+)$/`) before calling `Number()`. Non-matching input now falls through to the existing keep-as-string path, so the typed text is submitted verbatim and the gateway's schema validation rejects it with a visible error instead of silently storing a reinterpreted number.

This mirrors the merged nondecimal-reject pattern: #107480 (`parseCronEveryMs` rejects `0x10`/`1e3`/`+1` in cron repeat amounts) and #105158 (`parseStrictFiniteNumber` rejects hex `--cpus 0x10` in fleet). Exponent notation is treated as nondecimal per #107480: `1e3` stays a string rather than persisting `1000`. The shared `parseStrictFiniteNumber` helper was deliberately not used here because it accepts scientific notation, while the config form follows #107480's stricter spelling-preserving contract. Leading `+` is rejected (JSON number grammar has no `+` sign); negative decimals, floats, and `.5`/`5.` spellings coerce exactly as before, and the existing finite/integer guards are untouched.

No new config/env/options; the production change is one module-level regex plus one guard clause.

## User Impact

- Typing `0x10`/`0b1010`/`1e3` into a numeric config field no longer silently writes a different number into `openclaw.json`; the typed text is preserved and rejected by schema validation where the user can see it.
- Valid decimal input (`42.5`, `-7`, `.5`) behaves exactly as before.

## Evidence

### Production-entry proof — real `createRuntimeConfigCapability` save flow

A standalone script (not committed) drives the real capability — `ensureLoaded` + `ensureSchemaLoaded` + `patchForm` + `save()` against a plain fake gateway client object — and inspects the exact `raw` bytes submitted to `config.set`. No test mocks anywhere in the path.

Before fix (`origin/main` @ `19b5e564d7`):

```json
{
  "hex-into-number-field": { "typed": "0x10", "submittedValue": 16, "submittedType": "number" },
  "binary-into-integer-field": { "typed": "0b1010", "submittedValue": 10, "submittedType": "number" },
  "exponent-into-number-field": { "typed": "1e3", "submittedValue": 1000, "submittedType": "number" },
  "hex-into-string|number-union": { "typed": "0x10", "submittedValue": 16, "submittedType": "number" },
  "valid-decimal-still-coerces": { "typed": "42.5", "submittedValue": 42.5, "submittedType": "number" },
  "valid-negative-still-coerces": { "typed": "-7", "submittedValue": -7, "submittedType": "number" }
}
```

After fix (this PR @ `17f11f49d6`):

```json
{
  "hex-into-number-field": { "typed": "0x10", "submittedValue": "0x10", "submittedType": "string" },
  "binary-into-integer-field": { "typed": "0b1010", "submittedValue": "0b1010", "submittedType": "string" },
  "exponent-into-number-field": { "typed": "1e3", "submittedValue": "1e3", "submittedType": "string" },
  "hex-into-string|number-union": { "typed": "0x10", "submittedValue": "0x10", "submittedType": "string" },
  "valid-decimal-still-coerces": { "typed": "42.5", "submittedValue": 42.5, "submittedType": "number" },
  "valid-negative-still-coerces": { "typed": "-7", "submittedValue": -7, "submittedType": "number" }
}
```

### Control-red

The two outputs above are the same script on the same inputs. Reverting this PR (deleting the `CONFIG_FORM_DECIMAL_NUMBER_RE` guard so line 372 is again a bare `Number(trimmed)`) reproduces the silent `16`/`10`/`1000` rewrites; with the guard, typed spellings survive verbatim into the submitted payload for schema validation to reject.

### Regression tests — `ui/src/lib/config/index.test.ts`

- `it.each(["0x10", "0b1010", "0o17", "1e3", "+5"])`: number AND integer fields keep the typed spelling as a string in the submitted `config.set` payload.
- `it.each([["42.5", 42.5], ["-7", -7], [".5", 0.5]])`: valid decimal spellings still coerce to numbers.

### Test suite

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run ui/src/lib/config/index.test.ts

      Tests  74 passed (74)
```

### Lint

`tsgo -p tsconfig.ui.json`: 0 errors in `ui/`. The same run reports 3 pre-existing errors in `packages/net-policy/src/ip.ts` caused by stale `ipaddr.js@1.9.1` in this worktree's reused `node_modules` (net-policy on main requires `ipaddr.js@2.4.0` since #892c460ce8); that file is untouched by this PR and does not import the changed code.

Real gateway from this branch's `dist/` + real Chromium driving the served Control UI (no mocks): on `origin/main` coercion, typing `1e5` into a union-typed byte-size field autosaves and silently persists `100000`; with this PR the same input shows "Save failed" + Retry and persists nothing, while `100000` saves as a number. target.title: fix: guarded fetch falls back to IPv6 when IPv4 is unreachable
target.body:
Closes #87763

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where guarded provider requests on dual-stack hosts can fail when IPv4 is unreachable even though IPv6 is available.

## Why This Change Was Made

Single-address pinned lookups remain IPv4-only when IPv4 records exist, preserving the behavior introduced for #80078. All-record lookups used by Node/Undici Happy Eyeballs now receive the complete SSRF-validated, IPv4-first pinned record set, so IPv6 remains available as a fallback. Explicit-family and hostname-fallback behavior are unchanged.

## User Impact

Users on networks where a provider's IPv4 route is unavailable but IPv6 works can complete guarded provider requests without disabling DNS pinning or weakening resolved-address checks.

## Evidence

- Updated `src/infra/net/ssrf.pinning.test.ts` proves:
  - repeated single-address lookups stay on IPv4;
  - `{ all: true }` returns IPv4 and IPv6 in IPv4-first order;
  - explicit family 6 still returns IPv6.
- `git diff --check` passes.
- A source-aware Codex review found no actionable regression.

target.title: fix(agents): Responses turns that end incomplete report zero tokens and zero cost
target.body:
Closes #100954

## What Problem This Solves

When an OpenAI/Azure Responses turn ends with `response.incomplete` — the `max_output_tokens` and
`content_filter` cases, and what Azure emits on early truncation — the agent records **zero tokens and
zero cost** for that turn. The tokens were spent and billed; the session transcript, `usage.cost` RPC and
usage bars just do not see them, so per-session accounting drifts low every time a turn is truncated.

This is the drift reported in #100954.

## Why This Change Was Made

`processResponsesStream` in `src/agents/openai-responses-transport.ts` had a terminal branch for
`response.completed` only:

```ts
} else if (type === "response.completed") {
  ...
  if (usage) { output.usage = { ... } }
  calculateCost(model as never, output.usage as never);
  output.stopReason = mapResponsesStopReason(response?.status as string | undefined);
}
```

`response.incomplete` matched no branch in the chain, so the event was silently dropped: `output.usage`
was never written, `output.stopReason` never set. Unlike the package-side processor, this one has no
"stream ended before a terminal response event" guard, so nothing surfaced the miss — the loop just ended
and the turn was reported as free.

**The package side already fixed exactly this.** #109615 finalizes both terminal events through one
`finalizeResponse` (`packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-shared.ts:963`), which records usage,
cost and service-tier pricing. It did not touch the agent path, and that path is live for the
`openclaw-openai-responses-transport` / `openclaw-azure-openai-responses-transport` runtimes — the Azure
one being #100954's subject. So this is a sibling-parity fix: same bug, same shape of fix, the surface
#109615 left behind.

The recording moves into `src/agents/openai-responses-terminal-outcome.ts` rather than growing
`openai-responses-transport.ts`, which is a legacy file the max-lines ratchet will not let grow. Pulling
the block out drops it from **2502 to 2444 lines**, so the ratchet gets slack instead of pressure.

`reasoningTokens` stays agent-local on purpose: the package-side `Usage` type does not carry it, which is
why the two processors keep separate helpers rather than sharing one.

### Content-filtered turns

Routing `response.incomplete` through the terminal path would otherwise map a content-filtered turn to a
plain `length` stop, while the package side reports it as a provider error
(`openai-responses-shared.ts:991-997`). Rather than leave the two terminal surfaces disagreeing, this
mirrors the package behavior — `stopReason: "error"` with `Provider incomplete_reason: content_filter`.
That is the one behavior here that is not purely additive, and it is pinned by a test.

## Evidence

**The added tests fail on `origin/main` and pass here.** On main the assertions report exactly the
symptom from #100954:

```
× records Responses usage and cost when the turn ends incomplete
    AssertionError: expected +0 to deeply equal 50        <- usage.input is 0 on main
× reports content-filtered incomplete Responses turns as errors
    AssertionError: expected 'stop' to be 'error'
```

The usage test drives the real `processResponsesStream` with an Azure Responses model and an exact
`response.incomplete` event (`max_output_tokens`, populated usage with cached + cache-write tokens), then
asserts the split buckets and priced cost. Sub-cent totals round to zero at `toBeCloseTo`'s default
precision, so it also asserts `toBeGreaterThan(0)`.

**On proof shape:** #109615 pinned the identical package-side behavior with a synthetic terminal event
(`it("finalizes incomplete terminal events with usage")`,
`packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-shared.test.ts:1281`) rather than a captured provider
transcript. These tests are the same shape against the agent processor.

```
openai-transport-stream*.test.ts + openai-responses*.test.ts   695 passed | 0 failed (18 files)
max-lines ratchet                        OK (openai-responses-transport.ts 2502 -> 2444)
dead-export ratchet (knip)               0 entries
oxlint / oxfmt --check                   clean
tsgo core + test-src                     no errors
```

## Merge Risk

Low. One terminal branch and one extracted helper; no signature, type, config or protocol change. The
`response.completed` path is byte-for-byte the same logic, just relocated — the 695 existing tests across
the transport suites cover it and are unchanged.

The only behavior that moves is the case this fixes: `response.incomplete` now records usage/cost and
sets a stop reason instead of being dropped. Turns that previously reported zero will now report their
real tokens, so per-session totals go **up** for truncated turns — that is the correction, and it is worth
calling out for anyone watching usage dashboards.

This supersedes the agent-side half of #101608, which I opened before #109615 landed the package-side fix;
that PR is now conflicted and half-redundant, so I am closing it in favor of this narrower one.

AI-assisted.

target.title: fix(agents): agent-created files get lowercased names on Windows
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

On Windows, files and directories an agent creates get **lowercased names**. Ask for
`src/Components/MyComponent.tsx` and what lands on disk is `src\components\mycomponent.tsx`.

NTFS is case-insensitive but case-*preserving*, so nothing fails locally — the agent reads its own file
back fine. The damage shows up downstream: git records the lowercased name, and the TypeScript/React
import the agent just wrote (`./Components/MyComponent`) resolves on the author's Windows box but breaks
for every teammate on Linux/macOS and in CI. Any agent-authored name that is not already lowercase is
affected: `README.md`, `Dockerfile`, `MyClass.ts`.

For some names it is worse than a case change. `"İstanbul.md".toLowerCase()` is `"i̇stanbul.md"` —
U+0130 becomes the two code points U+0069 U+0307, one longer than the original and not reversible. So a
Turkish filename does not come back lowercased, it comes back **corrupted**.

This is Windows-only. The POSIX branch of the same function preserves case correctly today.

## Why This Change Was Made

`toRelativePathUnderRoot` (`src/agents/path-policy.ts:76-90`) ran both root and candidate through
`normalizeWindowsPathForComparison` and then **returned** the resulting relative path:

```ts
const rootForCompare = normalizeWindowsPathForComparison(rootResolved);
const targetForCompare = normalizeWindowsPathForComparison(resolvedCandidate);
const relative = path.win32.relative(rootForCompare, targetForCompare);
return validateRelativePathWithinBoundary({ relativePath: relative, ... });
```

That helper lowercases (`@openclaw/fs-safe@0.4.1`, `dist/path.js:17` →
`normalizeLowercaseStringOrEmpty(...)`). Lowercasing is right for a **comparison key** — which is exactly
how the other two call sites use it — but this function hands the relative path back to callers, and they
build files out of it:

- `src/agents/agent-tools.read.ts:1089-1092` — `mkdir`: `path.resolve(root, relative)` → `fs.mkdir`
- `src/agents/agent-tools.read.ts:1059-1060` — `writeWorkspaceFile` → `.write(relative, { mkdir: true })`
- `src/agents/apply-patch.ts:310,318,326` — `apply_patch` writeFile / remove / mkdirp

`toCanonicalRelativeWorkspacePath` (`agent-tools.read.ts:1167-1179`) does not rescue it: `fs.realpath`
restores the true case only of the **already-existing** ancestor, the new basename stays lowercased, and
line 1179 re-lowercases the whole thing on the way out. `assertSandboxPath` does not either — it is
handed the already-derived `resolved` path, not the original candidate.

The lowercasing was also never needed for the boundary math. `path.win32.relative` already matches the
root case-insensitively **and** returns the tail in its original case, so the pre-lowercasing bought
nothing and cost the filename. The one part of that normalization the boundary check does rely on is
extended-length prefix stripping — without it a `\\?\C:\...` candidate relativizes to
`..\..\..\?\C:\...` and gets rejected as an escape. So this adds `normalizeWindowsPathPreservingCase`
next to the comparison variant in `src/infra/path-guards.ts`. It mirrors that helper step for step —
including the trim — minus the lowercasing, and a test pins that equivalence directly so the two cannot
drift:

```ts
expect(normalizeWindowsPathPreservingCase(input).toLowerCase()).toBe(
  normalizeWindowsPathForComparison(input),
);
```

### Sibling surfaces

All three callers of `normalizeWindowsPathForComparison` were checked. Only this one was misusing it:

| Call site | Uses result as | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `src/plugins/installed-plugin-index-record-reader.ts:215` | comparison key (`===`) | correct, untouched |
| `isPathInside` (fs-safe) | discards relative, returns boolean | correct, untouched |
| `src/agents/path-policy.ts` | **returns it to callers** | fixed here |

## Evidence

**Live before/after on real Windows** (Windows 11, NTFS, Turkish locale), driving the real
`toRelativeWorkspacePath` through the exact call pattern of `agent-tools.read.ts`, then reading the names
back with `fs.readdirSync`:

Before (`origin/main`):

```
--- case 1: agent asked for src\Components\MyComponent.tsx ---
  toRelativeWorkspacePath -> "src\components\mycomponent.tsx"
  ON DISK                 -> components/mycomponent.tsx

--- case 2: agent asked for İstanbul.md ---
  asked   : İstanbul.md  | length 11 | U+0130
  ON DISK : i̇stanbul.md | length 12 | U+0069 U+0307
  identical? NO  <- filename corrupted, not just lowercased
```

After (this branch):

```
--- case 1: agent asked for src\Components\MyComponent.tsx ---
  toRelativeWorkspacePath -> "src\Components\MyComponent.tsx"
  ON DISK                 -> Components/MyComponent.tsx

--- case 2: agent asked for İstanbul.md ---
  asked   : İstanbul.md | length 11 | U+0130
  ON DISK : İstanbul.md | length 11 | U+0130 U+0073
  identical? YES
```

**Why the existing test did not catch it:** `path-policy.test.ts:23` used an all-lowercase candidate
(`c:/users/user/openclaw/memory/log.txt`), which passes either way. The new cases use mixed case.

**Tests** — every added mixed-case assertion fails on `origin/main` and passes here:

```
path-policy.test.ts + path-guards.test.ts        41/41 passed
+ agent-tools.workspace-paths, apply-patch,
  installed-plugin-index-record-reader            111 passed | 12 skipped, 0 failed
max-lines ratchet                                 OK
dead-export ratchet (knip)                        0 entries
oxlint / oxfmt --check                            clean
tsgo -p tsconfig.core.json                        no errors in touched files
```

## Merge Risk

Low, but this touches a sandbox boundary, so here is the containment argument explicitly.

**The boundary decision is unchanged.** `path.win32.relative` compares case-insensitively, so
`relative(lower(a), lower(b))` and `relative(a, b)` return the same *structure* — same number of `..`
segments, same segment count, same absoluteness. Only the case of the returned characters differs.
`validateRelativePathWithinBoundary` looks at exactly that structure (`""`/`"."`, `".."`, `"../"`,
`"..\\"`, `isAbsolute`), so every accept/reject verdict is identical. Verified empirically:

```
root: C:\Users\User\OpenClaw
escape, no lowercasing        -> "..\Other\log.txt"     still rejected
root itself, differing case   -> ""                     allowRoot still honored
drive-letter case c: vs C:    -> "Memory\Log.txt"       still matched
\\?\ prefix NOT stripped      -> "..\..\..\?\C:\..."    why stripping is kept
```

Two of the added tests pin this directly — an escape that differs from the root only by case is still
rejected, and a differently-cased root still resolves to `""` under `allowRoot`. Both pass before and
after the change, which is the point.

Scope is one file's Windows branch plus one new helper with a single caller. POSIX behavior is untouched.

AI-assisted.

target.title: fix(auto-reply): deliverBindingPayload missing abortSignal check
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Plugin binding notifications could still be delivered via `routeReplyToOriginating`, `dispatcher.sendToolResult`, or `dispatcher.sendFinalReply` after the dispatch operation has been aborted, because `deliverBindingPayload` did not check or propagate the dispatch abort signal. The same gap existed in the fast-abort acknowledgment path: it propagated `abortSignal` but lacked a post-route guard before the direct-dispatcher fallback.

## Why This Change Was Made

`deliverBindingPayload` was missing the same abort-signal guard that `sendPayloadAsync` (the sibling function) already implements. Aligned them by adding:

1. **Pre-check**: `getDispatchAbortSignal()` + `.aborted` early return
2. **Propagation**: pass `abortSignal` to `routeReplyToOriginating` options
3. **Post-check**: after the async `routeReplyToOriginating` call, check `.aborted` again before falling through to `sendToolResult`/`sendFinalReply`

The fast-abort acknowledgment path had the same pattern: it propagated `abortSignal` through `routeReplyToOriginating` but did not re-check after the await, so a cancellation during routed delivery could still reach `dispatcher.sendFinalReply` on the wrong surface.

Since all callers of `deliverBindingPayload` are in the same closure that already has `getDispatchAbortSignal()`, no parameter changes were needed.

## User Impact

Users of plugin bindings may see fewer stale/misdirected binding notifications when a dispatch operation is aborted (e.g. session timeout, manual cancellation). The fast-abort acknowledgment is similarly guarded against wrong-surface delivery after cancellation. No behavior change for normal (non-aborted) dispatch paths.

## Evidence

### Test results

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
    src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.test.ts \
    src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.acp-abort.test.ts \
    src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.reply-dispatch.test.ts \
    src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.lifecycle-and-bindings.test-utils.ts

 ✓ 3 files  →  311 tests passed (311)
```

### Lint and type checks

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `tsgo:core` (type) | ✅ |
| `test-types` | ✅ |
| `oxlint` | ✅ |
| `oxfmt` | ✅ |

### Mid-route abort regression (deliverBindingPayload post-check)

Abort fires synchronously inside `routeReply` mock, simulating the race window:

```
[C] 1. AbortController created (signal.aborted = false)
[C] 2. routeReply mock invoked — firing abortController.abort()
[C] 5. Calling dispatchReplyFromConfig with abortSignal...
[C] 6. Result: {"queuedFinal":false,"counts":{"tool":0,"block":0,"final":0}}
[C] 8. sendFinalReply NOT called:  ✓ (post-check guard active)
[C] 🎯 VERDICT: Binding reply was SUPPRESSED (no delivery)
```

### E2E QA gateway proof (pre-aborted signal)

Real QA bus server + real `handleQaInbound` + real `dispatchReplyWithBufferedBlockDispatcher`:

```
 ✓ |extension-qa| proof-109109-abort-gateway.test.ts (1 test)

[E2E] QA bus started: http://127.0.0.1:42989
[E2E] abortSignal:    aborted = true
[E2E] ✅ routeReply NOT called (short-circuited at entry guard)
[E2E] ✅ Binding reply SUPPRESSED
```

### Fast-abort post-route guard

After the `routeReplyToOriginating` await returns null, `getDispatchAbortSignal()?.aborted` is checked before the `dispatcher.sendFinalReply` fallback, preventing wrong-surface delivery when cancellation races with the route.

## Files changed

| File | ± | Change |
|------|---|--------|
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.ts` | +19/−1 | deliverBindingPayload pre/post abort checks + signal propagation; fastAbort path signal propagation + post-route guard |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.lifecycle-and-bindings.test-utils.ts` | +98 | Regression test: mid-route abort race window in plugin binding delivery |
| `extensions/qa-channel/src/inbound.ts` | +3 | Optional `abortSignal` parameter on `handleQaInbound`, forwarded into dispatch `replyOptions` |

target.title: fix(ui): neutralize spreadsheet formulas in usage CSV export
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Control UI usage page lets operators download session and daily cost data as CSV (`ui/src/pages/usage/view.ts` export menu → `buildSessionsCsv` / `buildDailyCsv` in `ui/src/pages/usage/query.ts`). Two cell-safety corners in `csvEscape` were missing:

1. **Spreadsheet formula injection.** `session.label` is user/agent-controlled (stored via the gateway session store, `src/gateway/server-methods/usage.ts`), and `agentId` / `channel` / `model` flow through the same row builder. A label starting with `=`, `+`, `-`, `@` (or their full-width forms), optionally preceded by whitespace/tab, is executed as a formula when the exported CSV is opened in Excel/LibreOffice/Numbers — the classic CSV injection vector (e.g. a label of `=HYPERLINK(...)`).
2. **Bare carriage return breaks rows.** The quote trigger `[",\n]` did not include `\r`, so a label containing a lone `\r` was emitted unquoted and split the row in strict CSV parsers.

## Why This Change Was Made

`csvEscape` now runs every cell through `neutralizeSpreadsheetFormulaCell` (prepend a leading `'` when the cell, after optional leading whitespace, starts with a formula prefix) and the quote trigger covers `\r` as well. This is a direct mirror of the merged google-meet attendance CSV fix https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109725 (formula neutralization) and its follow-up https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109926 (`\r` quoting), keeping one canonical cell-safety pattern across the repo. The same fix for this site was previously proposed in https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/44376, which was auto-closed by the contributor queue cap (`too-many-prs`), not rejected on merit.

No behavior changes for ordinary cells: values without a formula prefix and without `"\r\n,` bytes render byte-identical to before. Regression coverage locks neutralization for ASCII and full-width prefixes, whitespace-prefixed formulas, tab/newline-led cells, and bare `\r` quoting.

Fix classification: additive hardening of an existing export path; no config, API, or SDK surface changes.

## User Impact

- Exported usage CSVs can no longer smuggle executable spreadsheet formulas through session labels or ids.
- Labels containing carriage returns no longer corrupt row boundaries when the CSV is re-imported.

## Evidence

Base: `f104c51e8598edd6786f1e790b7cff582edda0b8` (`origin/main`). Head: `1ba58657d7e7dd3fdb7871b242898cbf600b2dc1`.

### Behavior — before / after (same inputs through `buildSessionsCsv`)

| Input label | Before (main @ f104c51e85) | After (this PR) |
|---|---|---|
| `=HYPERLINK("https://evil.example","click")` | emitted raw, executes on open | `'=HYPERLINK(...)` neutralized |
| `  =1+1` / `\t=1+1` | emitted raw | `'  =1+1` / `'\t=1+1` neutralized |
| `＝1+1` (full-width) | emitted raw | `'＝1+1` neutralized |
| `line1\rline2` | unquoted, row splits | `"line1\rline2"` quoted |
| `Session 1` (ordinary) | unchanged | unchanged (existing test still green) |

### Tests

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/pages/usage/query.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  10 passed (10)
```

### Control-red (fix reverted, same test file)

```

```

### Lint / whitespace

```

$ git diff --check                                                      # clean
```

### Impact surface

| Surface | Status |
|---|---|
| `ui/src/pages/usage/query.ts` `csvEscape` | neutralize + `\r` quoting added |
| `ui/src/pages/usage/query.ts` `buildSessionsCsv` / `buildDailyCsv` | unchanged call sites; all cells flow through `csvEscape` |
